prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I broke at last the terror-fringed fascination that bound my ancient gaze to those crowding faces of plunder and seized my remnant life in a miracle of decision between white- collar hands and shook it like a cheap watch in my ear and threw it down beside me on the earth floor and rose to my feet. I made of their shoulders and heads bobbing up and down a new ladder and leaned it on their sweating flanks and ascended till midair my hands so new to harshness could grapple the roughness of a prickly day and quench the source that fed turbulence to their feet. I made a dramatic descent that day landing backways into crouching shadows into potsherds of broken trance. I flung open long-disused windows and doors and saw my hut new-swept by rainbow brooms of sunlight become my home again on whose trysting floor waited my proud vibrant life.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker finally breaks free from a fear-filled fascination with the threatening crowd.
- The speaker seizes control of his remaining life through a sudden and decisive act of will.
- The speaker rises above the crowd by turning their bodies into a symbolic ladder.
- The speaker disrupts the source of the crowd’s violent energy and descends from his trance-like state.
- The speaker reopens his neglected home and rediscovers a proud, vibrant life waiting there.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The speaker confronts a paralyzing fear of predatory, crowding forces and breaks free through a decisive act of self-reclamation and symbolic ascent. This liberation restores clarity, agency, and a renewed sense of home, transforming a place of trance and terror into one filled with light and vibrant life.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: I broke at

outputs.L1:
At last, I broke the terror-fringed fascination that had bound my ancient gaze to those crowding faces of plunder. I seized my remnant life, in a miraculous act of decision, between white-collar hands; shook it like a cheap watch against my ear; and cast it down beside me on the earthen floor before rising to my feet. I fashioned from their bobbing shoulders and heads a new ladder, leaned it against their sweating flanks, and climbed until, suspended in midair, my hands—so unaccustomed to harshness—could grasp the roughness of a prickly day and extinguish the source that fed turbulence to their feet.  

That day, I made a dramatic descent, landing backward into crouching shadows, into the potsherds of a broken trance. I flung open long-disused windows and doors, and saw my hut—newly swept by the rainbow brooms of sunlight—become my home again, upon whose trysting floor my proud, vibrant life awaited me.
outputs.L2: At last, I tore myself free from the fear-edged spell that had held my aged eyes fixed on those pressing faces of robbery. With an astonishing act of will, I grasped what was left of my life in my white-collar hands, rattled it beside my ear like a worthless watch, then cast it onto the earthen floor beside me and stood up. Using their rising and falling heads and shoulders as though they were the rungs of a newly made ladder, I propped it against their sweating sides and climbed until, suspended in the air, my hands—unused to such rough work—could seize the thorny hardness of the day and stop the force that was driving unrest into their feet. That day I came down with theatrical suddenness, falling backward into hunched shadows and into the shattered fragments of a broken enchantment. I threw wide the windows and doors that had long been unused, and I saw my hut, freshly swept by sunlight like rainbow-colored brooms, turn once more into my home; there, on the floor of meeting, my proud and pulsing life was waiting for me.
outputs.L3:
The speaker finally breaks free from his fear-filled fascination with the threatening crowd. Until this point, he has been almost hypnotized by their violence and power, unable to look away even though their presence fills him with dread. The crowd seems to dominate his imagination, holding him in a state of paralysis. However, this moment marks a turning point: he stops being merely a frightened observer and begins to act.

Through a sudden and decisive act of will, the speaker seizes control of what remains of his life. Rather than surrendering to panic or allowing the crowd to determine his fate, he chooses movement, resistance, and self-command. This decision is not gradual or hesitant; it comes as a sharp break from passivity. In taking action, he reclaims his agency and asserts that his life still belongs to him.

The speaker then rises above the crowd by turning their bodies into a symbolic ladder. This image suggests both physical escape and spiritual or psychological elevation. The very people who once seemed to trap and threaten him become the means by which he climbs beyond them. By using the crowd in this way, he transforms a source of fear into a path toward freedom. Their collective force no longer crushes him; instead, it enables his ascent.

In doing so, the speaker also disrupts the source of the crowd’s violent energy. His action breaks the spell that has held him in a trance-like state, separating him from the emotional intensity and chaos that surrounded him. As he descends from this heightened, almost dreamlike condition, he returns to himself with a clearer sense of purpose. The crowd’s power over him weakens because he no longer feeds it with fear or fascination.

Finally, the speaker reopens his neglected home and rediscovers the proud, vibrant life that has been waiting there. The home represents more than a physical place; it stands for identity, memory, stability, and self-respect. By returning to it, he reconnects with the parts of himself he had abandoned or forgotten. What seemed empty or lost is revealed to be full of life. The speaker’s journey, therefore, ends not simply in escape from the crowd, but in a renewed embrace of his own strength, dignity, and belonging.
outputs.L4:
The speaker begins in a state of intense fear, surrounded by forces that feel predatory, crowded, and overwhelming. These forces seem to press in from every side, creating a sense of paralysis and helplessness. The world around the speaker is not merely frightening but almost hypnotic, as though it has placed them under a trance. They feel trapped in a space where danger is everywhere, where movement is difficult, and where their own sense of self has been weakened by terror.

Yet the speaker does not remain powerless. At a crucial moment, they recognize that escape depends on an act of inner strength. They must reclaim themselves from the fear that has held them captive. This act of self-reclamation is decisive: it marks the moment when the speaker refuses to be controlled by the threatening forces around them. Instead of submitting to the darkness, they rise above it, both literally and symbolically. The ascent represents freedom, courage, and the recovery of personal agency.

Through this liberation, the speaker’s perception of the world changes. What was once a place of confusion, trance, and terror becomes clear and alive again. The oppressive atmosphere lifts, and light returns. The speaker regains the ability to see, choose, and act. Their surroundings are no longer defined by fear but by vitality and possibility.

In the end, the experience transforms the meaning of home. Home is no longer a place associated with entrapment or danger; it becomes a space of renewal, brightness, and belonging. The speaker’s journey is therefore not only an escape from external threats but also a restoration of the self. By confronting fear and breaking free from its hold, they recover clarity, agency, and a renewed sense of life.
outputs.L5:
**I Broke At**

I broke at the moment I realized I had been carrying too much for too long.

It wasn’t loud. There was no dramatic collapse, no shattered glass, no warning sign flashing in the distance. I simply reached a point where my heart could no longer pretend it was fine. The weight of expectations, disappointments, and silent struggles became too heavy to hold.

I broke at the edge of exhaustion, where strength began to feel like a mask. I had smiled through pain, answered “I’m okay” when I wasn’t, and kept moving even when every part of me wanted to stop. But breaking was not the end of me.

It was the beginning of honesty.

In that moment, I learned that being broken does not mean being weak. Sometimes it means you have survived more than anyone could see. Sometimes it means your soul is asking for rest, healing, and kindness.

I broke at the place where I needed to change. And slowly, piece by piece, I began to rebuild—not into who I was before, but into someone softer, wiser, and more real.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single paragraph in a dense, lyrical postcolonial style about a person breaking free from a hypnotic crowd, reclaiming their hut and their life.
counterfactuals.output: At dusk, when the crowd still swayed beneath the loudspeakers like a field of obedient cane, their mouths sugared with slogans not their own, she felt the spell crack inside her like a dry seed remembering rain; and though the drummers of the new masters beat time from the old verandas, though the flags changed colors while the hunger kept its familiar teeth, she stepped out of that human tide, out of the dust raised by marching feet and borrowed dreams, and walked toward the hut they had named worthless, primitive, backward, the hut her grandmother had plastered with river clay and songs. Behind her the multitude murmured in one throat, calling her traitor, madwoman, ghost, but she had already begun to hear herself again: the small sovereign pulse beneath the ribs, the language hidden under the tongue like an ember. She pushed open the raffia door and entered not a ruin but a republic of breath—calabash, mat, smoke-blackened beam, the stubborn pot waiting for fire—and there, in the tender darkness, she took back her body from command, her name from inventory, her future from the ledger of men who had mapped her life in ink and appetite. Outside, the crowd continued its trance, circling the square where power wore a borrowed crown; inside, she lit the hearth, and the first flame rose slender and defiant, writing on the walls the old truth no empire could translate: that home is not the place left behind, but the place from which one refuses, at last, to be driven.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a surreal first-person literary passage where the narrator escapes a state of fear and fascination, climbs over a mob, shuts off the source of chaos, and returns home transformed.
counterfactuals.output:
I do not know whether I fled from terror or toward it. At the time the two were married inside me, fear and fascination turning one another’s faces with the same cold hand. I had stood too long in the square beneath that impossible tower, listening to the siren bloom from its iron throat. The sound did not merely enter the ear; it unfolded behind the eyes. It made windows tremble like trapped birds. It made strangers kneel, laugh, bite their knuckles, kiss the stones. Above us the great red lamp revolved, painting every face first with blood, then with carnival.

I had been among them, astonished, afraid to move because everything was moving: the statues weeping soot, the fountains running upward, the clouds crowding low as if to hear better. Then someone screamed my name, though I recognized no mouth. That was enough. The spell cracked.

I began to climb.

There was no stairway, no clear path, only bodies: shoulders, hats, raised arms, backs arched in devotion or panic. I stepped upon a broad man’s coat as if it were a hillside, seized the collar of a woman who was singing in a language of bells, and hauled myself upward. No one resisted. They swayed beneath me, a living sea, and I crossed them like a guilty saint in muddy shoes. Fingers clutched at my ankles, not to stop me but to be carried along. I could not carry them. I had only my two hands and the terrible certainty that the tower was not a tower at all, but an instrument, and that something unseen had been playing us.

At the base of it I found a door no larger than a child’s coffin. I crawled through. Inside, the siren’s cry became a solid thing, a white animal pressed against my chest. Gears turned in the dark, slick with moonlight. A brass lever shuddered at the center of the chamber, and beside it a little plaque read: CONTINUE.

I laughed then—not bravely, not sanely, but with the relief of discovering that chaos, too, can have a handle.

I pulled the lever down.

The silence struck harder than the noise. Outside, the mob collapsed into individuals. The fountains remembered gravity. The red lamp dimmed, embarrassed by its own drama. People looked at their hands, at one another, at the sky, as if returning from separate dreams and finding themselves dressed for the wrong century.

I walked home through streets still warm with hallucination. My door recognized me reluctantly. In the mirror, my face was the same, except that my eyes had gone a little farther away. I washed the dust of strangers from my palms, but something of them remained: their weight, their fear, their upward reaching.

That night my house seemed smaller, yet kinder. The ticking clock no longer sounded like time escaping, but like a creature breathing in its sleep. I had left home as one more trembling citizen of the square. I returned with silence folded inside me, dark and usable, and when dawn came to the window, I did not bow to it.

I opened it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Rewrite the moment of awakening from communal madness as high modernist prose, using vivid metaphors like ladders made of bodies, sunlight as brooms, and life as something reclaimed.
counterfactuals.output:
At first there was only the murmur, that old black weather of the mind, passing from mouth to mouth like smoke in a sealed room. We had stood in it so long we mistook it for air. Each face had become a mask worn by another mask; each hand, lifted, pointed where all hands pointed; each cry rose because the cry before it had risen. We were a crowd, yes, but also a single fever, a single animal dreaming itself enormous and righteous.

Then—no trumpet, no command—only a faltering.

One voice broke. Not loudly. It fell inward, like a cup slipping from a table in another room. And through that small fracture came the first thin blade of morning.

We saw, with the terror of the newly sighted, what we had made of ourselves: ladders made of bodies, each back bent for another’s ascent; shoulders bruised into rungs; the fallen pressed flat into usefulness. How eagerly we had climbed. How holy the height had seemed when seen through the red gauze of frenzy. But now the tower trembled, and every rung had a name, every name a mother, a hunger, a childhood, a grave waiting with its mouth open.

Sunlight entered then—not as blessing, not as gold, but as brooms. It swept the square. It swept the dust from eyelids, the slogans from tongues, the sleep from the blood. It went under doors and into collars, found the hidden corners where obedience had nested, and brushed out the last gray feathers of the collective dream. We blinked beneath its labor. We were ashamed of the brightness.

No one knew who first knelt. Perhaps all of us did, in the same shattered instant. We descended from one another. We unclasped our fingers from throats, from banners, from stones. The human ladder loosened and became again a multitude of separate spines, separate wounds, separate astonished hearts. Someone began to sob; someone laughed as if laughter were an artifact unearthed after centuries; someone called a stranger brother and meant not the word of the mob, but the word before the mob had stolen it.

Life returned, not as conquest, not with drums, but like a field reclaimed from floodwater: slow, shining, strewn with wreckage, stubbornly green beneath the mud. We gathered it in handfuls. We lifted it from gutters. We found it still breathing under the heap of our certainties.

And when we rose, we did not rise as one.

That was the miracle.

We rose as many.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an Achebe-inspired allegorical monologue about a colonized or intimidated speaker overcoming terror, dispersing plunderers, and rediscovering dignity in their home.
counterfactuals.output:
When the locusts first came, we mistook their wings for rain.

They arrived with bright teeth and iron voices, measuring our courtyards with their boots, naming our rivers as if water had been born on their tongues. They entered my father’s house and pointed to the rafters, the goats, the carved stool, the clay pot where my mother kept the sacred seed. “These are now under our protection,” they said, and their protection had the weight of a stone on the chest.

I was afraid. Let no one say fear is not a real thing. Fear has hands. It closes the mouth. It teaches the knees to bend before the mind has agreed. For many seasons I walked softly in my own compound, as though my footsteps were trespassing. I watched strangers carry away our yams, our bronze, our names. I watched them laugh at the drum because they did not understand that a drum can speak.

But a man who sleeps in a burning hut must one day choose between ashes and the door.

The turning came at dawn, when I saw my youngest child playing beside the threshold with a broken mask—one of the old masks they had torn down and thrown aside. She held it to her face and asked, “Whose eyes are these?”

Then I knew that terror had eaten enough.

I went first to the central fire, where the old men sat with silence folded around them. I did not shout. A river does not announce its depth by noise. I said, “The hawk has carried the chick because the hen forgot her claws.” One by one they lifted their heads. The women came from the grinding stones. The youths came from the paths. Even those who had hidden their anger under obedience brought it out like a blade cleaned after long burial.

When the plunderers returned, they found no scattered household waiting to be counted. They found a village standing in its doorway.

We did not become what they were. We did not burn for the joy of burning or steal because theft had visited us. We beat the drums they had mocked. We raised the songs they had called noise. We named each stolen thing before reclaiming it, so that the world would know it had belonged to someone. The carved stool came home. The seed pot came home. The bronze faces, green with sorrow, came home. And those who had strutted through our courtyards discovered that a people may be bent for a season and still rise like grass after the elephant has passed.

By sunset, the road that had brought them was full of their retreat.

That night I entered my house not as a guest, not as a shadow, but as the child of those who built it. I touched the wall and felt my own pulse answer from the clay. My mother’s pot stood again in its corner. My father’s stool faced the fire. The mask was mended and hung where the ancestors could see us.

I learned then that dignity is not given back like a coin dropped into the palm. It is remembered. It is called by its true name. It is taken up from the dust with both hands.

And now, when the wind moves through the rafters, I do not hear the wings of locusts.

I hear the house breathing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poetic prose excerpt, no dialogue, in which an ancient-gazed narrator breaks a trance, rises from an earth-floored hut, opens long-closed windows, and finds their vibrant life waiting.
counterfactuals.output:
I came back to myself as a stone remembers rain.

For a long while, I had sat in the earth-floored hut with my hands open upon my knees, my sight fixed inward, where centuries drifted like ash across a dead fire. Dust had gathered on my shoulders. Roots had whispered beneath the packed clay. The roof-beams, dark with smoke and age, leaned above me like tired elders, and the air was thick with the breath of closed seasons. In that stillness, I had forgotten the weight of my own body, forgotten the small urgencies of blood, forgotten that the world was not only memory and shadow.

Then something broke.

It was not a sound, nor a vision, but a loosening, as when ice gives way beneath the first insistence of spring. My eyes, old with looking past the edges of mortal hours, opened upon the hut as though seeing it for the first time. The bowl beside the hearth. The woven mat worn thin by waiting. The door-latch furred with rust. My feet, bare and dust-pale, pressed into the cool ground, and the ground answered. I rose slowly, joints creaking like branches after storm, and each breath returned to me green-edged and sharp.

The windows had been closed so long they seemed part of the wall. I lifted the wooden bars. I pushed against swollen frames. One by one, with sighs of wood and startled light, they opened.

Morning poured in.

It came gold and blue and mercilessly alive, spilling over the sill, striking the clay floor, climbing my hands. Outside, the grasses trembled with dew. Birds stitched bright cries through the air. The garden, which I had believed surrendered to bramble and sleep, had climbed into riotous bloom: marigold, bean-vine, scarlet poppy, the silver backs of leaves turning in the wind. Beyond it, the path curved toward hills washed clean by sun, and on the line where the meadow began, my life stood waiting—not as a ghost, not as a punishment, but as a field uncut, a river unspent, a door left open by a patient and radiant world.

I leaned into the light, and the light knew me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
